newsitem.title: FRANCE: French leftists confident as poll campaign ends.
newsitem.headline: French leftists confident as poll campaign ends.

text.p: A confident French left on Friday urged voters to widen its first-round election upset in Sunday's parliamentary runoff contest while the ruling right exhorted them to keep the Socialist-Communist alliance out of power.
"I ask French men and women...to confirm and amplify the first-round vote," Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, 59, said in a statement as campaigning drew to a close.

The conservatives' big guns issued anguished last-ditch appeals not to let "the trap slam shut", urging voters to think of the future rather than venting short-term irritation at record unemployment and austerity to fulfill the criteria for the single European Union currency.

Centrist ex-premier Raymond Barre, who imposed his own austerity plan in the late 1970s, issued a solemn appeal from his city hall in Lyon. "What is at stake is not a political changeover, the right or the left, but a decisive choice for our country," he said.

"Make sure that France does not wake up on Monday with a terrible hangover, realising that for the sake of voicing its bad mood it sentenced itself to five more years of Socialism," Philippe Seguin, the likely prime minister if the right wins, told his last campaign rally.
The left's first-round performance marked a stunning recovery since a 1993 rout ended a decade of Socialist rule.

But Seguin acknowledged he had had little time to convey his pledge to put jobs before austerity since he was anointed campaign leader after Prime Minister Alain Juppe took the blame for the first-round upset and bowed out.
"Time. This obsessive time. This time we need to say how well we understood the French people's message," he said.
Jospin said the choice was "between an outgoing majority which has failed and whose word can no longer be trusted and a new majority proposing real and positive change for the future".
The edgy Paris stock market closed 0.18 percent higher, as measure by the CAC 40 index, after shedding more than six percent earlier this week on prospects of a left-wing victory.
Mobbed by reporters, Jospin and Communist chief Robert Hue paraded together on a campaign trip to a poor northern Paris suburb despite strains within their election alliance.
Hue spelled out his terms for joining a possible Socialist-led government, including pay rises and new taxes on investment earnings, anathema to the ruling centre-right.
Jospin aides said he would reject any condition.
The two allies have bickered over European monetary union, which the Communists oppose but the Socialists generally favour.

After Jospin said a French left-wing win would stun and cheer Europe after Labour's victory in Britain, Seguin called the Jospin-Hue duo "ghosts from the past" and said they would only stun eastern Europe which had got rid of communism.

The left mocked the right's unlikely own duo of the socially minded Seguin and free-marketeer ex-finance minister Alain Madelin hastily anointed by President Jacques Chirac after Juppe said he would quit whatever the runoff result.

Jospin said that Chirac had gambled by calling the snap election, and, if the left won, he would have to "cohabit" with a left-wing government to the end of his term in 2002 rather than call another snap election in a year as he is entitled to do.

The last stretch of the campaign was marred by violence as two people, including a Socialist parliamentary candidate, were injured when anti-racist militants hurled eggs at Jean-Marie Le Pen and clashed with militants of his far-right National Front.

Le Pen, who was campaigning for his daughter Marie Caroline Le Pen in the troubled Paris suburb of Mantes-la-Jolie, denied throwing punches but admitted he had "slightly pushed" some people out of his way.
There was another clash in the southern town of Orange on Thursday night and police said two Front militants were slightly injured in a blaze set by arsonists at the local Front office.
Jospin also campaigned near Paris with his other ally, Greens leader Dominique Voynet, who said the ecologists, like the Communists, were pondering whether to join the cabinet if the left wins.
